Ishokori: The Spiritual Anatomy of the Annual Harvest Thanksgiving

By Grace Azi & Cultural Documentation Team

The annual Ishokori festival is the spiritual epicenter of the Anaguta calendar. Marking the culmination of the rainy season and the ripening of fonio (zana) and mountain sorghums, Ishokori is a profound synthesis of thanksgiving, royal blessing, and communal reconciliation.

The Blessing of the First Grain

Before any clan may consume the newly harvested grain, the paramount monarch—His Royal Majesty the Ujah of Anaguta—performs the ancient rite of pouring libation at the ancestral stone sanctuary in Naraguta. With ears of fonio elevated toward the sunrise, prayers are offered for sustained peace, maternal health, and seasonal fertility.

The Resonance of Animal-Horn Trumpets

No Ishokori is complete without the resonant drone of curved animal-horn trumpets, blown by guild members whose lineage has carried the breath of the ancestors for generations. The music begins at dawn, echoing off the granitic tors of the plateau to awaken the twelve clans for the central procession.

Communal Reconciliation

Beyond celebration, Ishokori serves as a sacred court of reconciliation. Any unresolved disputes between households or clans must be settled before sharing the communal feast, ensuring that no bitterness enters the new harvest year.
